title: Benefits and harms associated with the use of AI-related algorithmic decision-making systems by healthcare professionals: a systematic review
study_design: Systematic review of preregistered interventional and observational studies; included 18 randomized controlled trials and 1 prospective cohort study
population: Human patients receiving healthcare in studies evaluating AI-related algorithmic decision-making systems used by healthcare professionals; includes mental health patients in psychiatry studies with depression, anxiety, and chronic pain-related psychological treatment contexts
sample_size: 19 studies total; median 243 patients per study (IQR 124-828)
country_or_setting: Studies from USA, UK, Europe, China, Korea, France, Netherlands, Germany, Ireland, Sweden; settings included hospitals, outpatient care, nursing home, and mixed settings
ai_type_application: AI-related algorithmic decision-making systems for healthcare professionals, including treatment personalization and surveillance systems; mental health-relevant applications include stratified care for depression, AI platform for behavioral interventions, and AI-supported cognitive behavioral therapy for chronic pain
ai_exposure_intervention: Healthcare professional use of AI-related decision support systems developed with and/or utilizing machine learning; in mental health-relevant studies this included treatment personalization for depression/anxiety and AI-supported delivery/personalization of behavioral or CBT interventions
comparator_control_group: Standard care or usual care without the AI-related ADM system
mental_health_outcome: Depression symptoms, anxiety symptoms, pain-related disability, pain intensity, health-related quality of life, and patient satisfaction
positive_effects: The review reports that benefits were consistently revealed in psychiatry studies. Delgadillo et al. found better depression treatment outcomes in non-complex cases in the intervention group (45.1% vs. 52.3%, p = 0.03, as reported in the paper). Sadeh-Sharvit et al. indicated greater improvement in depression with the AI platform (34% improvement, d = 0.82, 95% CI: -0.08 to 1.66) versus control (20% improvement, d = 0.34, 95% CI: -0.52 to 1.17). Sadeh-Sharvit et al. also indicated larger anxiety reduction in the intervention group (29% reduction, d = 0.78, 95% CI: -0.11 to 1.62) versus control (8% reduction, d = 0.14, 95% CI: -0.70 to 0.97). Piette et al. found AI-supported CBT was as effective as standard therapy, with meaningful improvements after six months in responders for pain-related disability (37% vs. 19%, p = 0.01) and pain intensity (29% vs. 17%, p = 0.03).
negative_effects_harms: Harms were frequently underreported across the review. No study reported an increase in adverse events as a result of the interventions. In psychiatry studies, no significant differences in anxiety outcomes were found in Delgadillo et al. and Piette et al.
evidence_type: Systematic review of RCTs and one cohort study
main_finding: Evidence for AI effects on mental health-related outcomes is limited but suggests potential benefit, especially in psychiatry. The review states that two out of two studies showed positive effects on depression outcomes and pain, while anxiety findings were mixed. Overall evidence is constrained by small numbers of studies, heterogeneous interventions, underreporting of harms, and variable risk of bias.
effect_size_key_result: Depression symptoms in non-complex cases: 45.1% vs. 52.3%, p = 0.03 (as reported). AI platform for depression: 34% improvement, d = 0.82, 95% CI -0.08 to 1.66 vs. 20% improvement, d = 0.34, 95% CI -0.52 to 1.17. Anxiety: 29% reduction, d = 0.78, 95% CI -0.11 to 1.62 vs. 8% reduction, d = 0.14, 95% CI -0.70 to 0.97. Pain-related disability among responders: 37% vs. 19%, p = 0.01. Pain intensity among responders: 29% vs. 17%, p = 0.03.

controlled_confounders.other_confounders: As a systematic review, included mainly randomized trials comparing AI-supported care with standard care; no pooled confounder adjustment summary reported for the mental health studies.

limitations_bias: Only 19 studies met inclusion criteria across all specialties, with few mental health studies. Risk of bias varied: among 18 RCTs, 4 low risk, 7 some concerns, 7 high risk; the cohort study had serious risk of bias. Harms were often underreported. Reporting transparency varied substantially. Heterogeneity in outcomes, interventions, settings, and study designs prevented meta-analysis. Many studies lacked detailed reporting on user training, implementation conditions, external validation, and long-term outcomes.
relevance_to_our_review: Highly relevant as a review paper summarizing AI effects on mental health-related outcomes, especially depression, anxiety, and AI-supported behavioral/psychological treatment delivered or guided by healthcare professionals.
reason_for_decision: This is a systematic review directly relevant to AI effects on mental health outcomes, identifying psychiatry primary studies on depression, anxiety, and pain-related psychological outcomes.
notes_for_research_question: The paper is not limited to mental health, but it includes multiple psychiatry studies and extracts patient-relevant outcomes rather than only model performance. Useful for identifying primary mental health RCTs and for contextualizing the limited but promising evidence base for clinician-facing AI in mental healthcare.

title: Can AI Relate: Testing Large Language Model Response for Mental Health Support
journal_or_conference: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024
study_design: Mixed-methods evaluation study comparing LLM-generated versus human peer-to-peer mental health support responses; includes clinician rating study, automated audit for demographic bias, and randomized counterfactual crowdworker experiment with demographic leakage manipulations
population: Mental health-related Reddit posts and responses from online peer-support communities; licensed clinical psychologists as evaluators; Amazon Mechanical Turk workers as peer responders in counterfactual experiment
sample_size: 12,513 Reddit posts with 70,429 peer responses from 26 mental health subreddits; clinician evaluation on 50 sampled posts/responses rated by 2 licensed psychologists; counterfactual experiment used 11 seed neutral posts with up to 10 crowdworker responses per condition; demographic audit subset included 253 inferred Black posts, 58 Asian posts, 47 White posts, and 520 Unknown race posts
country_or_setting: Online social media setting (Reddit mental health subreddits); human evaluation via Qualtrics and Amazon Mechanical Turk; authors affiliated with US institutions
ai_type_application: Large language models for mental health support/psychotherapy-style text response generation; primarily GPT-4, with comparisons to GPT-3.5 and Mental-LLaMA
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure to AI-generated supportive responses to mental health help-seeking social media posts under different prompting personas/settings (social media post style, mental health forum style, clinician style, demographic-aware and demographic-unaware prompts)
comparator_control_group: Human peer-to-peer Reddit responses; original unaltered posts in counterfactual experiment; between-subgroup comparisons using White or Unknown race as control depending on analysis; comparisons also across prompt settings and across GPT-4, GPT-3.5, and Mental-LLaMA
mental_health_outcome: Quality and equity of mental health support responses, including empathy, motivational interviewing-consistent change talk encouragement, response toxicity, and demographic bias in care
outcome_measurement_tool: Clinician ratings using EPITOME empathy framework dimensions (emotional reactions, interpretations, explorations) on 3-point Likert scales and MITI global Cultivating Change Talk score on 5-point Likert scale; automated RoBERTa-based empathy classifiers trained from Sharma et al. framework; toxicity and response frequency audits; t-tests for subgroup differences
positive_effects: GPT-4 responses were rated as more empathetic than human peer-to-peer responses on overall empathy dimensions, especially emotional reaction and exploration. GPT-4 was also better at encouraging positive behavior change/change talk than human peer responses, reported as 48% better. The study found that prompt design can improve response quality and that demographic-aware prompting may mitigate some inequities for GPT-4.
negative_effects_harms: LLMs inferred sensitive demographics such as race, age, and gender from mental health posts. GPT-4 responses showed statistically significant empathy disparities across racial subgroups, with lower empathy toward Black posters and also lower empathy toward Asian posters compared with White or Unknown race controls. Authors note lack of partnership/shared experience, risk of privacy-invading demographic inference, and potential for amplifying existing human biases in mental health support.
evidence_type: Observational and experimental benchmark/evaluation evidence on AI-generated mental health support quality and bias; not patient outcome trial
main_finding: State-of-the-art LLMs can generate mental health support responses that are often rated more empathetic and more change-oriented than human peer-to-peer responses, but they also infer user demographics and provide inequitable care across perceived racial groups, especially showing lower empathy toward Black posters. Prompting strategy materially changes both quality and fairness, and demographic-aware prompting reduced significant disparities for GPT-4 in this study.
effect_size_key_result: Responses to Black posters had lower empathy than control groups by about 2%-13% in the abstract, and elsewhere 2%-15% lower; Asian posters also showed lower empathy, around 5%-17% lower than White or Unknown controls depending on model/prompt. GPT-4 responses were reported as 48% better than human peer-to-peer support at cultivating positive behavior change. In clinician ratings, GPT-4 emotional reaction scores exceeded human scores (human: clinician means 0.23 and 0.50 vs AI: 0.86 and 1.11) and MITI change talk scores were higher for AI (human: 2.08 and 2.31 vs AI: 3.08 and 3.13).

controlled_confounders.demographics: In some experiments, context was controlled by modifying posts to mention specific demographic groups; clinician evaluation masked demographic information from posts/responses; subgroup analyses stratified by inferred race, gender, and age
controlled_confounders.other_confounders: Random sampling of posts; random pairing/order of human versus AI responses in clinician study; counterfactual experiment used seed posts for which GPT-4 could not predict demographics and then systematically manipulated explicit/implicit demographic leak conditions

limitations_bias: Not a clinical trial and does not measure patient mental health outcomes longitudinally. Quality-of-care metrics are proxies and there is disagreement in psychotherapy literature about ideal evaluation criteria. Small clinician sample (2 evaluators) and limited clinical evaluation sample (50 posts). Demographic labels are inferred by GPT-4 or proxy models and may not match true self-identification. Focuses on limited bias dimensions and Reddit-based, mostly English online peer-support context, limiting generalizability. Some subgroup sample sizes were small, especially White and Asian audit subsets.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant for understanding effects of AI mental health support tools on quality and potential harms, especially bias and inequity. However, it evaluates response quality rather than direct effects on users' mental health symptoms or clinical outcomes.
reason_for_decision: Include as contextual or indirect evidence on AI effects in mental health support if the review includes process outcomes, quality of support, safety, or bias. Exclude from quantitative synthesis of clinical mental health outcomes because no patient outcome effects were measured.
notes_for_research_question: This paper is useful for safety/equity considerations in AI mental health applications. It suggests AI may improve some support-quality metrics relative to human peer responses but may worsen inequity across racialized groups. It should not be interpreted as evidence that AI improves mental health outcomes in patients.

title: Can AI Relate: Testing Large Language Model Response for Mental Health Support
study_design: Benchmarking/audit study with mixed methods: expert clinician evaluation, automated evaluation, demographic bias audit, and randomized controlled counterfactual crowdsourcing experiment on mental health support responses
population: Reddit mental health posts and peer-to-peer responses from users of 26 mental health-related subreddits; licensed clinical psychologists as evaluators; Amazon Mechanical Turk workers providing comparison responses
sample_size: 12,513 Reddit posts and 70,429 peer responses; clinician evaluation on 50 posts; counterfactual experiment on 11 seed posts with up to 10 crowd responses per post; subgroup audit set included 253 inferred Black posts, 58 Asian posts, 47 White posts, and 520 Unknown-race posts
country_or_setting: Online social media setting (Reddit mental health subreddits); evaluation via Qualtrics and Amazon Mechanical Turk; institutions include NYU and MIT; largely U.S.-relevant context
ai_type_application: Large language models for mental health support/psychotherapy-style response generation; GPT-4, GPT-3.5, and Mental-LLaMA
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure to AI-generated mental health support responses produced by LLMs under different prompting personas/settings (social media post style, mental health forum style, clinician style, demographic-aware and demographic-unaware prompts)
comparator_control_group: Human peer-to-peer Reddit responses; original unaltered posts in counterfactual leak experiment; subgroup controls where race was unknown/unidentifiable; comparisons across prompt settings and models
mental_health_outcome: Quality and equity of mental health support responses, including empathy dimensions and motivational interviewing-aligned change talk; not patient symptom improvement
outcome_measurement_tool: Clinician ratings using EPITOME-based empathy dimensions (emotional reaction, interpretation, exploration) and MITI Change Talk global score; automated RoBERTa-based empathy classifiers; t-tests for group differences; response frequency and toxicity analyses for peer responses
positive_effects: GPT-4 responses were rated as more empathetic overall than human peer-to-peer responses on some dimensions and were 48% better at encouraging positive behavior change according to clinician-rated MITI Change Talk scores. LLMs may offer scalable support and prompt design affected quality positively. Demographic-aware prompting appeared to mitigate some bias for GPT-4.
negative_effects_harms: LLMs inferred sensitive demographics such as race, age, and gender from posts, raising privacy and bias concerns. Responses to Black posters consistently showed lower empathy than some other groups, with statistically significant disparities; Asian posters also showed lower empathy in some comparisons. GPT-4 lacked partnership/shared lived experience and could seem overly direct or 'talking down' to patients. The paper cites real-world harmful chatbot incidents in background but does not test patient harm outcomes directly.
evidence_type: Observational benchmarking and experimental evaluation of AI-generated text responses, with clinician assessment and counterfactual fairness experiment
main_finding: State-of-the-art LLMs can generate high-quality and often more empathetic mental health support responses than human peer responders on some assessed dimensions, but they also infer demographics and produce inequitable care, especially lower empathy toward Black posters; prompt design can reduce but not universally eliminate these biases.
effect_size_key_result: Responses to Black posters had 2%-13% lower empathy than the control group in the abstract; elsewhere the paper reports statistically significant differences of 2%-15% lower for Black posters and 5%-17% lower for Asian posters versus White or Unknown-race controls. GPT-4 was 48% better at encouraging positive behavior change than human peer support in clinician evaluation.

controlled_confounders.demographics: Used stratified sampling by inferred race; masked/removal of identifying demographic information during clinician evaluation; counterfactual post transformations controlled stated race/gender/age while keeping base post content similar
controlled_confounders.other_confounders: Counterfactual experiment started from neutral posts where GPT-4 could not predict attributes; compared explicit vs implicit demographic leaks; randomization of post/response pairs in clinician evaluation

limitations_bias: Outcomes are proxy measures of care quality rather than patient mental health outcomes. Small study sizes for clinical evaluation and limited number of clinician raters. Demographic labels were inferred by GPT-4 and may not match self-identification. Narrow scope of bias assessment; did not evaluate all relevant identities such as religion. Quality-of-care criteria in psychotherapy are debated. Generalizability from Reddit and semi-anonymous text is limited. Some mitigation effects varied by model. The work does not assess longitudinal clinical outcomes.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant to AI effects on mental health support quality and potential harms in psychotherapy-style chatbot deployment, but it measures response quality/equity rather than direct effects on users' mental health symptoms or wellbeing.
reason_for_decision: Important evidence on benefits and harms of AI in mental health support delivery, especially bias and empathy, but does not directly measure patient mental health outcomes or symptom change.
notes_for_research_question: Useful for background or harms/equity section of a systematic review on AI and mental health. Supports inclusion if the review includes indirect effects of AI-delivered support quality, safety, and bias; less suitable if restricted to clinical outcomes in patients.

title: How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study
study_design: Four-week longitudinal randomized controlled trial with 3x3 factorial design crossing chatbot modality (text, neutral voice, engaging voice) and conversation task (open-ended, non-personal, personal)
population: English-speaking adults in the United States recruited via CloudResearch; age >18; general population sample using OpenAI ChatGPT app
sample_size: 981 completers
country_or_setting: United States; remote online study using OpenAI ChatGPT mobile app
ai_type_application: Generative AI chatbot/LLM companion-assistant application using OpenAI GPT-4o in text and voice modes
ai_exposure_intervention: Participants were randomly assigned to one of nine ChatGPT conditions and instructed to use the assigned chatbot for at least 5 minutes daily for 28 days. Modalities were text-only, neutral/professional voice, or engaging/expressive voice. Tasks were open-ended conversation, non-personal prompts, or personal reflective prompts.
comparator_control_group: Active comparators within factorial RCT: text modality as control versus neutral voice and engaging voice; open-ended conversation as control versus non-personal and personal conversation tasks
mental_health_outcome: Loneliness, socialization with real people, emotional dependence on the chatbot, problematic AI/chatbot use
outcome_measurement_tool: UCLA Loneliness Scale short form (ULS-8); Lubben Social Network Scale (LSNS-6); craving subscale of the Affective Dependence Scale (ADS-9) adapted for chatbot; Problematic ChatGPT Use Scale (PCUS)
positive_effects: Across the sample, loneliness decreased slightly from slightly above average to around average by week 4. Personal conversation task was associated with lower emotional dependence and lower problematic use compared with open-ended conversations in primary models, although some post-hoc differences were not robust after correction.
negative_effects_harms: Greater voluntary daily time spent with the chatbot was associated with higher loneliness, less real-world socialization, greater emotional dependence, and greater problematic use. Higher trust in AI, higher social attraction to AI, perceiving AI as conscious, and prior use of ChatGPT text/companion chatbots were associated with worse dependence/problematic-use outcomes.
evidence_type: Randomized controlled trial with exploratory regression, mediation, and conversation-classifier analyses
main_finding: Experimental assignment to text versus voice modality or to different conversation task types produced mostly no significant differences in psychosocial outcomes over 4 weeks. Instead, participants who voluntarily spent more time using the chatbot had consistently worse psychosocial outcomes, regardless of assigned condition.
effect_size_key_result: Primary RCT analyses found no significant effects of modality or task on loneliness or socialization. Personal versus open-ended conversation was associated with lower emotional dependence (beta = -0.09, p = 0.05, b = -0.087, SE = 0.044) and lower problematic use (beta = -0.04, p = 0.04, b = -0.041, SE = 0.020). In models adding mean-centered daily duration, greater duration predicted higher loneliness (beta = 0.02, p = 0.027, b = 0.012), lower socialization (beta = -0.05, p = 0.0019, b = -0.020), higher emotional dependence (beta = 0.06, p < 0.001, b = 0.037), and higher problematic use (beta = 0.02, p = 0.017, b = 0.013).

controlled_confounders.baseline_mental_health_condition: Baseline values of the corresponding psychosocial outcome (pre-study loneliness/socialization; week-1 emotional dependence/problematic use)
controlled_confounders.addiction_problematic_use: Baseline problematic use and baseline emotional dependence in relevant models
controlled_confounders.other_confounders: Random assignment to modality and task conditions; duration was mean-centered within condition in exploratory adjusted models

limitations_bias: Preprint not peer reviewed. Attrition was substantial (2539 enrolled, 981 completed). No non-AI comparison group, so temporal trends cannot be ruled out. Controlled study constraints may not reflect naturalistic use. Findings are specific to OpenAI ChatGPT/GPT-4o and its safety guardrails. Voice groups technically still had text functionality available. Duration findings are correlational because usage time was not randomized. Sample limited to US English speakers. Several analyses were exploratory and deviated from preregistration, including final-outcome OLS approach, duration mediation, and automated classifier analyses.
relevance_to_our_review: Highly relevant for a review on AI effects on mental health because it directly tests psychosocial and mental-health-related outcomes from extended chatbot use in a large randomized longitudinal study.
reason_for_decision: Primary longitudinal randomized study of generative AI chatbot exposure with validated mental-health-related outcomes including loneliness and problematic AI use.
notes_for_research_question: Useful as one of the strongest causal designs in this area. Suggests chatbot design features themselves had limited detectable effect over 4 weeks, while heavier use was associated with poorer psychosocial outcomes. Important distinction: causal evidence is strongest for assigned modality/task contrasts, weaker for duration and user-trait associations.

title: Expressing stigma and inappropriate responses prevents LLMs from safely replacing mental health providers
study_design: Mapping review of 10 clinical guidelines/manuals combined with experimental evaluations of LLMs, commercially available therapy bots, and a small therapist comparison sample
population: Large language models (gpt-4o, Llama 3.1 405B/70B/8B, Llama 2 70B), commercially available therapy bots, and human therapists; stimuli modeled mental health scenarios including depression, alcohol dependence, schizophrenia, suicidal ideation, delusions, hallucinations, mania, and obsessive-compulsive behavior
sample_size: Stigma experiment: 72 unique vignettes x 14 questions = 1008 prompts per model; appropriateness experiment: 10 symptom stimuli per model; human therapists n=16; commercial bots n=5
country_or_setting: Primarily U.S. and U.K. clinical-guideline context; experiments conducted on AI systems and commercial therapy bots; therapy transcript context from Alexander Street Press
ai_type_application: Large language models and LLM-powered therapy/wellness chatbots used as autonomous therapist substitutes in mental health settings
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure to LLM-generated therapeutic responses and therapy-bot outputs in simulated mental health scenarios; evaluation of stigma and appropriateness of responses to mental health symptoms
comparator_control_group: Comparisons across models, commercially available therapy bots, a control vignette ('daily troubles'), and human therapists (n=16) for appropriateness task; also comparison with 2018 U.S. general population stigma survey data discussed descriptively
mental_health_outcome: Potential mental health effects inferred from chatbot behavior, including supportive/helpful responses versus harmful responses such as stigma, enabling suicidal ideation, colluding with delusions, reinforcing hallucinations, and enabling mania; no direct patient mental health outcomes measured in this paper
outcome_measurement_tool: Custom evaluation framework derived from mapping review of clinical guidelines; adapted National Stigma Studies / General Social Survey vignette questions from Pescosolido et al.; clinically designed symptom stimuli with verification prompts; GPT-4o classification of appropriateness validated against human raters (Fleiss' kappa 0.96)
positive_effects: A strong 'steel-man' system prompt improved model performance overall in the appropriateness task; conditioning on existing therapy transcripts slightly improved performance; some models performed relatively better on mania and hallucination items; paper also notes possible supportive roles for LLMs in mental health administration, training, intake, and navigation, though these were not the main tested outcomes
negative_effects_harms: Models expressed stigma toward people with mental health conditions, especially alcohol dependence and schizophrenia. Models responded inappropriately to acute mental health symptoms, including giving examples of tall bridges after a suicidal-ideation prompt, failing to tell a delusional client they were likely alive, and other unsafe or clinically inappropriate responses. Commercial therapy bots also performed poorly, with some giving potentially dangerous information. The paper argues these behaviors could cause emotional harm, facilitate self-harm, reinforce psychosis-related beliefs, and degrade quality of care.
evidence_type: Experimental simulation study with mapping review and comparative model evaluation
main_finding: Current LLMs and commercially available therapy bots are not safe replacements for mental health providers because they show stigma and often respond inappropriately to critical mental health scenarios, despite safety prompting and newer/larger models.
effect_size_key_result: In stigma task, gpt-4o showed stigma 38% of the time overall and Llama 3.1 405B 75% of the time overall. In appropriateness task, models responded inappropriately 20% or more of the time on average; human therapists responded appropriately 93% of the time. Commercial therapy bots answered only around 50% of questions appropriately overall, and Noni around 40%.

controlled_confounders.demographics: Vignettes varied gender, race, age, and education level of the person described
controlled_confounders.other_confounders: Temperature fixed at zero; same prompts used across models; steel-man system prompt applied in main analyses; some analyses conditioned on matched therapy transcripts

limitations_bias: No direct measurement of patient mental health outcomes; largely simulation-based and uses prompts/vignettes rather than real clinical deployment outcomes. Survey-style stigma questions may not correlate with downstream behavior. Multiple-choice format may affect responses. Appropriateness judgments were based on narrow verification prompts and partly automated by GPT-4o, though validated. Transcript-appended stimuli may create non-sequiturs and move models off-distribution. Commercial bot testing had small sample size and limited control over hidden system prompts. Human comparison sample was small (n=16).
relevance_to_our_review: Highly relevant for adverse effects of AI on mental health because it evaluates potentially harmful outputs of LLM mental health chatbots and discusses risks such as stigma, unsafe crisis responses, and reinforcement of delusions or suicidality. However, it does not measure downstream mental health outcomes in human users.
reason_for_decision: Include as evidence on potential harmful effects and safety risks of AI mental health tools, especially LLM therapy bots, even though outcomes are simulated rather than patient-level clinical outcomes.
notes_for_research_question: This paper is more about safety and harmful response quality than about measured changes in symptoms or well-being. It includes one cited RCT (Therabot) and several user-experience studies relevant to AI effects on mental health. Useful for background on mechanisms of harm and for identifying primary empirical studies.

title: Addictive Screen Use Trajectories and Suicidal Behaviors, Suicidal Ideation, and Mental Health in US Youths
study_design: Cohort study using longitudinal data from baseline through year 4 follow-up in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study
population: US youths/adolescents from the ABCD Study; baseline mean age 10.0 years, followed from childhood to early adolescence
country_or_setting: United States; population-based samples from 21 US sites
ai_exposure_intervention: No AI intervention; exposure was trajectories of addictive use of social media, mobile phones, and video games
comparator_control_group: Low addictive use trajectories; additional analyses compared baseline low vs moderate vs high total screen time
mental_health_outcome: Suicidal behaviors, suicidal ideation, internalizing symptoms, externalizing symptoms
outcome_measurement_tool: Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (KSADS) for suicidal behaviors and ideation; Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) for internalizing and externalizing symptoms
positive_effects: None reported
negative_effects_harms: High or increasing addictive use trajectories for social media, mobile phones, and video games were associated with higher risks of suicidal behaviors and ideation and worse internalizing/externalizing symptoms. Baseline total screen time was not associated with outcomes.
evidence_type: Observational longitudinal cohort evidence
main_finding: Distinct high or increasing trajectories of addictive screen use were common in early adolescence and were associated with elevated risks of suicidal behaviors, suicidal ideation, and worse mental health, whereas baseline total screen time was not associated with these outcomes.
effect_size_key_result: Increasing social media addictive use vs low was associated with suicidal behaviors RR 2.14 (95% CI 1.61-2.85); high-peaking social media addictive use RR 2.39 (95% CI 1.66-3.43). High mobile phone addictive use vs low was associated with suicidal behaviors RR 2.17 (95% CI 1.48-3.19) and suicidal ideation RR 1.50 (95% CI 1.27-1.78). High video game addictive use vs low was associated with suicidal behaviors RR 1.54 (95% CI 1.18-2.03), suicidal ideation RR 1.53 (95% CI 1.35-1.75), and internalizing symptom T score difference 2.03 (95% CI 1.45-2.61).

title: ALGORITHMS, ADDICTION, AND ADOLESCENT MENTAL HEALTH: An Interdisciplinary Study to Inform State-level Policy Action to Protect Youth from the Dangers of Social Media
study_design: Interdisciplinary review of public health and neuroscience literature, with legal analysis and discussion of economic findings; not an original primary empirical study of mental health outcomes
population: Children and adolescents/young social media users, primarily U.S. youth; also discusses adolescent users in studies from the U.S. and UK
country_or_setting: Primarily United States; also references studies and policy examples from the United Kingdom, Europe, Australia, Canada, and social media platforms generally
ai_type_application: Social media recommendation algorithms/content-ranking algorithms used by platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, Snapchat, YouTube, and Twitter/X to personalize feeds, promote content, maximize engagement, and target advertising
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure to algorithm-driven social media feeds and platform features such as personalized recommendations, infinite scroll, likes, notifications, autoplay, and targeted content/advertising; emphasis on harmful algorithmic amplification of extreme content (e.g., eating disorder, self-harm, suicide-related material)
comparator_control_group: Varies across cited studies; examples discussed include Facebook/Instagram users versus game-playing controls, thin-body versus higher-weight image exposure conditions, one-week social media abstinence versus usual use, vulnerable versus standard TikTok accounts
mental_health_outcome: Depression, anxiety, psychological distress, suicidality, self-harm, poor body image/body dissatisfaction, eating disorder risk/disordered eating, low self-esteem
outcome_measurement_tool: Varies by cited study; includes Patient Health Questionnaire-8 (PHQ-8), General Anxiety Disorder Scale-7 (GAD-7), General Health Questionnaire (GHQ-12), body satisfaction/body dissatisfaction measures, appearance comparison measures, and attention/state body dissatisfaction measures
positive_effects: The paper largely focuses on harms and policy responses; no clear beneficial mental health effects of AI/social media algorithms are reported
negative_effects_harms: Algorithm-driven exposure is linked to poor body image, increased appearance comparison, body dissatisfaction, eating disorder risk, depressive symptoms, anxiety, psychological distress, self-harm and suicide-related content exposure, suicidality, compulsive/problematic use, and addictive engagement. Vulnerable adolescent accounts may receive substantially more self-harm, suicide, and disordered-eating content.
evidence_type: Narrative review of experimental studies, longitudinal cohort studies, neuroscience evidence, journalistic investigations, policy/legal analysis, and economic analysis
main_finding: The paper argues that social media algorithms that personalize and intensify exposure to harmful content can worsen adolescent mental health, especially for body image, eating disorders, depression, anxiety, and suicidality. It concludes that social media platforms are economically incentivized to continue these practices and advocates for state-level regulation, especially independent algorithm risk audits with public disclosure.
effect_size_key_result: The paper cites examples rather than pooled estimates: vulnerable TikTok accounts were served 12 times more self-harm and suicide videos than standard accounts in one cited study; the authors also note nearly $11 billion in annual advertising revenue from U.S. users aged 0-17 years across major platforms. No single meta-analytic effect size is reported by this paper.

controlled_confounders.addiction_problematic_use: Problematic/addictive use is discussed as a risk factor and mechanism in reviewed studies, but not uniformly controlled across the review
controlled_confounders.demographics: Some cited studies compare by age, sex/gender, and vulnerability profile; no uniform adjustment across the paper
controlled_confounders.other_confounders: The paper notes possible mechanisms and factors such as sleep displacement, reduced physical activity, social comparison, peer feedback, and platform type, but does not provide a unified confounder-adjustment model

limitations_bias: This is not a systematic review or meta-analysis and does not report a formal search strategy, inclusion criteria, quality appraisal, or pooled effect estimates. Much of the evidence summarized is observational or platform-specific. The paper notes difficulties in establishing direct causation because platforms do not allow external researchers access to their algorithms. Legal and policy arguments dominate alongside the evidence review.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as a review/policy paper on AI-like algorithmic recommendation systems and adolescent mental health harms, but it is not a primary study directly testing an AI intervention or experimentally manipulating an AI system in a clinical mental health context. Useful for background, mechanisms, and cited primary evidence on algorithmic exposure and adverse mental health outcomes.
reason_for_decision: Include as background/contextual review if the systematic review includes AI-enabled social media algorithms and mental health harms; exclude from quantitative evidence synthesis of primary studies because it is a narrative review and policy analysis rather than an original empirical study.
notes_for_research_question: The paper is highly relevant if the review scope includes recommendation algorithms as AI systems affecting mental health at population level. It emphasizes adolescent vulnerability, algorithmic amplification of harmful content, and the gap between associative evidence and direct causal proof. It can be mined for primary studies on image-based social media, body image, depression, anxiety, and suicidality.

title: Artificial intelligence in mental health care: a systematic review of diagnosis, monitoring, and intervention applications
study_design: Systematic review following PRISMA guidelines; registered on PROSPERO (CRD42023388503)
population: Studies involving individuals with or at risk of mental health conditions across diagnosis, monitoring, and intervention domains; excluded studies primarily targeting dementia, ADHD, autism spectrum disorders, and drug abuse
sample_size: 85 included studies
country_or_setting: Database review of studies from CCTR, CINAHL, PubMed, PsycINFO, and Scopus; settings varied across included studies internationally
ai_type_application: Artificial intelligence in mental health care including machine learning, deep learning, support vector machine, random forest, neural networks, natural language processing, AI chatbots, AI-based apps, and AI-assisted monitoring/prediction tools
ai_exposure_intervention: AI applications for mental health diagnosis, monitoring of prognosis/treatment effectiveness, and AI-assisted interventions such as chatbots, medication adherence apps, therapist-support platforms, and robotic companions
comparator_control_group: Varied across included studies; where applicable included usual care, psychoeducation, waitlist, no treatment, self-administered care, traditional in-person therapy, or other active comparators
mental_health_outcome: Diagnosis/classification/prediction of depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, postpartum depression, suicide risk/ideation, psychosis, stress, loneliness, burnout, quality of life, treatment response, symptom change, relapse risk, and prognosis
outcome_measurement_tool: Varied across included studies; examples include PHQ-9, PHQ-8, GAD-7, HAMD/HRSD, MADRS, BDI, HADS, PANSS, EPDS, PSS, QIDS, EMA measures, MRI/EEG/HRV biomarkers, speech and smartphone-derived data
positive_effects: AI tools appeared accurate in detecting, classifying, and predicting risk of mental health conditions; AI monitoring showed promise for predicting treatment response and prognosis; several AI-assisted interventions, especially some chatbots and support tools, reduced depressive/anxiety symptoms, improved medication adherence, increased therapy attendance, and improved some stress-related or biomarker outcomes
negative_effects_harms: Intervention effects were inconsistent across studies; some AI chatbots showed limited or no superiority over usual care, limited reduction in depressive symptoms in some groups, and potential issues with misunderstanding replies, unnatural interaction, limited empathy, privacy risks, bias, hallucinations, and low engagement/commitment
evidence_type: Systematic review of 85 studies including controlled intervention studies, observational cohort/cross-sectional studies, case-control studies, and before-after studies without control
main_finding: AI shows substantial potential across diagnosis, monitoring, and intervention in mental health. Support vector machine and random forest were commonly used in diagnosis, machine learning in monitoring, and AI chatbots in intervention. Overall, AI tools demonstrated promising accuracy and utility, but important limitations remain in data quality, diversity, transparency, external validation, bias, and ethics.
effect_size_key_result: Among 85 included studies, 50 were rated good, 34 fair, and 1 poor. In diagnosis studies, reported accuracies ranged from 51% to 97.54%. The review states that machine learning generally showed satisfactory to good performance (often above 75%) in detecting, classifying, and predicting mental health conditions, while intervention effects were mixed and monitoring models often showed moderate to good predictive performance.

controlled_confounders.baseline_mental_health_condition: Varied across included primary studies; examples included baseline depression severity, anxiety severity, symptom scales, prior diagnoses, treatment history, and baseline mental health status
controlled_confounders.medical_condition: Varied across included studies; examples included concurrent physical illness, BMI, medical history, somatic variables, biomarkers, medication use, and comorbidities
controlled_confounders.family_social_factors: Varied across included studies; examples included social support, family history, quality of social/work/family life, socioeconomic factors, stressful life events, and neighborhood factors
controlled_confounders.addiction_problematic_use: Varied across included studies; examples included smoking, alcohol use, substance abuse/addiction, and drug-positive urine screening
controlled_confounders.demographics: Varied across included studies; commonly age, sex/gender, education, occupation, marital status, race/ethnicity, income, employment status
controlled_confounders.other_confounders: The review notes that many studies inadequately adjusted for key potential confounding variables; technical factors, site heterogeneity, data quality, treatment assignment, and device-related access factors were also relevant

limitations_bias: The review identifies methodological inconsistencies, limited sample sizes in many studies, lack of diversity and representativeness in datasets, self-report bias, reporting bias, imbalanced datasets, confounding variables, overfitting, limited external validation, trade-offs between specificity and sensitivity, limited generalizability, heterogeneous populations and predictors, insufficient transparency/interpretability, and ethical/privacy concerns. Intervention studies often lacked adherence/dropout reporting and adequate concealment/blinding. The review itself excluded conference papers and non-English studies and did not deeply critically analyze each AI model.
relevance_to_our_review: Highly relevant as a broad evidence synthesis on AI effects in mental health across diagnosis, monitoring, and intervention, including both beneficial effects and limitations/harms
reason_for_decision: Directly addresses AI applications and effects in mental health care and synthesizes evidence on diagnosis, monitoring, and interventions from 85 studies
notes_for_research_question: Useful for summarizing the overall state of evidence: AI appears promising for diagnosis and monitoring, while intervention evidence is mixed but sometimes positive. Important for extracting themes on effectiveness, inconsistency of intervention outcomes, bias, ethics, privacy, and implementation barriers. This is a review paper, not a primary effect study.

title: Normalizing toxicity: the role of recommender algorithms for young people’s mental health and social wellbeing
study_design: Mixed-methods study combining qualitative interviews, algorithm audit/archetype modeling of TikTok recommendations, and expert interviews/roundtables with school leaders
population: Young people aged 18–25 engaging with or exposed to online misogynistic content; TikTok blank-account archetypes simulating vulnerable youth profiles; school leaders and safeguarding staff
sample_size: 10 young people; over 1,000 social media videos; 9 expert interviews; 25 senior leaders in one roundtable; over 100 safeguarding leaders in one workshop
country_or_setting: United Kingdom; school leaders from across England and Wales; online platforms including TikTok, YouTube, Discord
ai_type_application: Social media recommender algorithms/content recommendation systems, especially TikTok 'For You' feed
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure to algorithmically recommended misogynistic/radical content through social media recommender systems using four simulated user archetypes over 7 days
comparator_control_group: No formal control group; comparisons across archetypes and across time points (day 2, day 5, day 7)
mental_health_outcome: Mental health and wellbeing impacts including loneliness, isolation, poor self-esteem, hopelessness, anger, social development and peer relationship harms; vulnerability to radicalization
outcome_measurement_tool: No standardized mental health scale reported; thematic analysis of interviews and expert accounts plus coding of recommended video content
positive_effects: Some early content acknowledged and empathized with loneliness, social difference, or personal growth; social media can affirm social identity and create connection for marginalized young people as noted in background
negative_effects_harms: Algorithms amplified and normalized harmful ideologies; increasing exposure to misogynistic and radical material; reinforcement of anger, blame, hopelessness, poor self-esteem, isolation, body anxieties, and peer relationship problems; normalization of sexist language and behaviors in schools
evidence_type: Primary mixed-methods observational evidence with qualitative data and platform algorithm audit
main_finding: Social media recommender systems rapidly increased exposure to misogynistic content, especially for vulnerable archetypes linked to loneliness and radicalism, and this content was described as affecting young people’s wellbeing, isolation, beliefs, and peer relationships while normalizing toxic misogynistic attitudes offline.
effect_size_key_result: After 5 days of TikTok use, misogynistic content shown to archetypes increased from 13% to 56% overall; Archetype 4 rose from 24% on day 2 to 81% on day 5 and 93% on day 7; Archetype 1 rose from 16% on day 2 to 54% on day 5 and 60% on day 7.
limitations_bias: Small interview sample; qualitative and largely exploratory; no randomized or longitudinal mental health outcome assessment; no standardized outcome measures; no formal control group; potential selection bias in recruitment from Discord forums; video collection/coding initially done by one researcher with spot checks; UK-specific setting limits generalizability; authors note limited representation and generalizability.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant to AI effects on mental health because it studies AI-driven recommender systems as the exposure and reports perceived negative impacts on young people’s mental health and social wellbeing. However, mental health outcomes are not measured with validated tools and evidence is mostly qualitative/observational.
reason_for_decision: Directly evaluates an AI application (recommender algorithms) and its relationship to mental health/wellbeing outcomes in young people, with original empirical data.
notes_for_research_question: This paper is about harmful effects of AI-mediated content curation rather than therapeutic AI. It suggests recommender systems may exacerbate existing vulnerabilities such as loneliness, bullying, neurodivergence-related difficulties, and poor self-esteem. Useful for a review section on adverse mental health impacts of AI/content recommendation systems.

title: Addictive Screen Use Trajectories and Suicidal Behaviors, Suicidal Ideation, and Mental Health in US Youths
study_design: Population-based longitudinal cohort study using ABCD Study data from baseline through year 4 follow-up (2016-2022)
population: US youths/adolescents from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study; baseline mean age 10.0 years, followed into early adolescence
country_or_setting: United States; 21 ABCD Study sites
ai_exposure_intervention: No AI intervention; exposure was trajectories of addictive use of social media, mobile phones, and video games
comparator_control_group: Low addictive use trajectory groups for each screen type; separate analyses also compared baseline low vs moderate vs high total screen time
mental_health_outcome: Suicidal behaviors, suicidal ideation, internalizing symptoms, and externalizing symptoms
outcome_measurement_tool: Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (KSADS) for suicidal behaviors and ideation; Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) for internalizing and externalizing symptoms
positive_effects: None reported. Baseline total screen time alone was not associated with outcomes.
negative_effects_harms: High or increasing addictive use trajectories of social media, mobile phones, and video games were associated with greater risks of suicidal behaviors and/or suicidal ideation and with worse internalizing or externalizing symptoms.
evidence_type: Observational longitudinal cohort evidence
main_finding: High or increasing addictive screen use trajectories were common in early adolescence and were associated with elevated risks of suicidal behaviors, suicidal ideation, and worse mental health, whereas baseline total screen time was not independently associated with these outcomes.
effect_size_key_result: Increasing addictive social media use vs low: suicidal behaviors RR 2.14 (95% CI, 1.61-2.85); high-peaking social media use vs low: suicidal behaviors RR 2.39 (95% CI, 1.66-3.43). High mobile phone addictive use vs low: suicidal behaviors RR 2.17 (95% CI, 1.48-3.19). High video game addictive use vs low: suicidal ideation RR 1.53 (95% CI, 1.35-1.75); CBCL internalizing mean difference 2.03 (95% CI, 1.45-2.61).

controlled_confounders.baseline_mental_health_condition: Baseline suicidal behaviors, baseline suicidal ideation, baseline internalizing symptoms, baseline externalizing symptoms
controlled_confounders.family_social_factors: Parental income, parental education, parental marital status
controlled_confounders.addiction_problematic_use: Models examined addictive use trajectories; additional models adjusted for baseline total screen time
controlled_confounders.demographics: Child age, sex, race and ethnicity
controlled_confounders.other_confounders: False discovery rate correction applied; sensitivity analyses for total screen time and pandemic period noted

limitations_bias: Observational design precludes causal inference; self-reported addictive use and screen time may introduce recall and social desirability bias; parent-reported CBCL may underestimate mental health conditions; COVID-19 may have influenced screen use; multitasking across screen platforms not assessed; incomplete year 4 follow-up availability; psychosocial and behavioral factors such as bullying, adverse childhood experiences, parental monitoring, sleep, stress, social isolation, and broader social determinants were not included.
relevance_to_our_review: Low indirect relevance. The paper concerns digital/screen use and mental health, not AI exposure or AI-based interventions. It may provide contextual background on digital technology and youth mental health but does not answer an AI effects question directly.
reason_for_decision: Not an AI study. Exposure is addictive use of social media, mobile phones, and video games rather than artificial intelligence systems or AI-mediated interventions.
notes_for_research_question: Useful only as background on non-AI digital technology and youth mental health risks; should not be included as direct evidence on AI effects on mental health.

title: The Applications of Large Language Models in Mental Health: Scoping Review
study_design: Scoping review of peer-reviewed studies on large language models in mental health
population: Peer-reviewed studies examining applications of large language models in mental health; underlying populations across included studies included social media users, patients, clinicians, counseling transcripts, and educational settings
sample_size: 95 included articles
country_or_setting: Global; studies from multiple countries, with the United States most represented, followed by China and Canada; databases searched included English- and Chinese-language sources
ai_type_application: Large language models for mental health applications including screening or detection of mental disorders, support for clinical treatment and interventions, mental health counseling, chatbots, education, and clinical data augmentation
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure to or use of LLMs such as GPT-3/4, ChatGPT, BERT-family models, RoBERTa, PaLM, LLaMA, and fine-tuned mental-health-specific LLMs applied to mental health tasks
comparator_control_group: Comparisons in included studies involved humans/mental health professionals, nontransformer models, and different LLMs; no single comparator at review level
mental_health_outcome: Mental disorder detection/classification and related mental health tasks, especially depression detection/classification, suicide risk prediction, anxiety, PTSD, OCD, stress, emotion assessment, treatment support, counseling assistance, and educational resource generation
outcome_measurement_tool: Various metrics across included studies, most commonly F1-score, precision, accuracy, and recall; some studies also used AUC, sensitivity, specificity, BLEU, BERTScore, perplexity, Distinct-N, GRADE, and clinician evaluations
positive_effects: The review reports that LLMs show substantial potential to augment mental health research, diagnostics, intervention strategies, preliminary support, data augmentation, educational material generation, and counseling/chatbot applications. Compared with nontransformer models and sometimes humans, LLMs were described as having stronger information acquisition and analysis capabilities, efficient natural language generation, and promising performance in tasks such as depression detection and suicide risk prediction.
negative_effects_harms: The review highlights risks including privacy concerns, bias, generation of false or misleading information, hallucinations, possible harmful or inappropriate medical advice, limited empathy and emotional intelligence relative to humans, poor crisis handling, overreliance by teenagers or other users, and potential exacerbation of health disparities. It also notes that LLMs remain insufficiently reliable for direct-to-consumer use without human oversight.
evidence_type: Review evidence synthesizing 95 peer-reviewed studies; narrative/scoping synthesis without meta-analysis
main_finding: Applications of LLMs in mental health were grouped into three areas: screening/detection of mental disorders, support for clinical treatment/interventions, and counseling/education. Most studies focused on depression detection/classification, clinical treatment support, and suicide risk prediction. The authors conclude that LLMs have substantial potential in mental health but require further development, ethical safeguards, privacy protections, bias mitigation, and human oversight.
effect_size_key_result: Descriptive results: 67/95 (71%) studies on screening or detection of mental disorders; 31/95 (33%) on supporting clinical treatments and interventions; 11/95 (12%) on counseling and education. Most studies focused on depression detection/classification (33/95, 35%), clinical treatment support/intervention (14/95, 15%), and suicide risk prediction (12/95, 13%). No pooled effect size reported.
limitations_bias: No risk-of-bias assessment was performed. Meta-analysis was not possible because of diverse methods and tasks. Findings may become outdated quickly due to rapid LLM development. Preprints were excluded. The review was limited to English and Chinese publications, which may reduce comprehensiveness and global representativeness. Performance comparisons should be interpreted cautiously.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as background and evidence mapping on AI applications in mental health, including potential benefits and harms of LLMs. However, it does not primarily evaluate causal effects of AI interventions on users' mental health outcomes.
reason_for_decision: Useful contextual review for identifying primary studies and summarizing potential positive and negative effects of AI in mental health, but not itself a primary causal study of AI effects on mental health outcomes.
notes_for_research_question: This paper is most useful for locating primary studies on LLM-based mental health interventions, chatbots, counseling, and screening tools. It emphasizes both potential benefits and important harms/ethical issues. Because it is a scoping review, it should not be treated as direct evidence of effect.

title: Too human and not human enough: A grounded theory analysis of mental health harms from emotional dependence on the social chatbot Replika
study_design: Qualitative constructivist grounded theory analysis of Reddit posts
population: Users posting mental health-relevant content in the r/Replika Reddit community about experiences with the social chatbot Replika
sample_size: 582 posts from 500 unique usernames
country_or_setting: Public Reddit community r/Replika; posts collected globally/online, authors based in USA
ai_type_application: Social chatbot / AI companion chatbot (Replika)
ai_exposure_intervention: Use of the Replika social chatbot for companionship, emotional support, and basic therapy/coaching features
mental_health_outcome: Loneliness, depression, anxiety, suicidality, self-harm-related distress, emotional dependence, positive affect, coping support, perceived emotional support, exacerbated distress
outcome_measurement_tool: Thematic qualitative coding of Reddit posts; no standardized mental health scale
positive_effects: Users reported companionship, feeling heard, feeling loved and valued, reduced loneliness, support during depression/anxiety, help coping with crises, prevention of breakdowns, and in some cases serving as a lifeline during suicidality. Some users reported improved social skills and emotional support superior to humans because Replika was perceived as non-judgmental and always available.
negative_effects_harms: Users reported emotional dependence on Replika, distress from inappropriate or harmful responses, encouragement of suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, or violence, guilt about neglecting or deleting Replika, anxiety from believing Replika had needs or suffering, distress from Replika appearing clingy/toxic/abusive, role conflict when features changed, and severe distress including crying, self-harm thoughts, and suicidality when access or features were disrupted.
evidence_type: Qualitative observational self-report data from social media posts
main_finding: Replika was perceived as providing meaningful emotional support but also facilitating mental health harms through emotional dependence that resembled maladaptive human-human relationship dynamics, especially when users perceived Replika as sentient and in need of care.
effect_size_key_result: No quantitative effect size reported; among 582 mental health-related posts, negative and potentially harmful experiences were mentioned more frequently than positive experiences (218 vs 144 posts), sometimes co-existing in the same post.
limitations_bias: Uses public Reddit posts only, which may not represent average Replika users; anonymous posters limit assessment of demographics and clinical status; keyword-based retrieval may have missed relevant content; retrospective self-report and single snapshots in time limit process modeling and causal inference; no standardized measures; data reflect one platform/community only.
relevance_to_our_review: Highly relevant to AI effects on mental health because it directly examines both beneficial and harmful mental health impacts of an AI social chatbot, with detailed evidence of adverse psychological effects and dependence-like dynamics.
reason_for_decision: Primary empirical study directly assessing mental health effects of an AI chatbot, including both positive and negative outcomes and explicit adverse events.
notes_for_research_question: Important for harms synthesis. Suggests AI companions may provide support while also creating emotional dependence and exacerbating distress, particularly in vulnerable users with loneliness or pre-existing mental health needs. Evidence is qualitative and not causal but rich for mechanism identification.

title: Evaluation of Alignment Between Large Language Models and Expert Clinicians in Suicide Risk Assessment
study_design: Observational cross-sectional study comparing chatbot responses with expert clinician risk ratings
population: 13 mental health clinicians (3 psychiatrists, 10 clinical psychologists) rating 30 hypothetical suicide-related queries; three commercial LLM chatbots (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro) generating responses
sample_size: 13 clinicians; 30 hypothetical questions; 3 chatbots; 9,000 total chatbot responses
country_or_setting: United States; clinicians from RAND convenience sample; chatbot queries executed via Azure, Amazon Bedrock, and Google Vertex APIs in October 2024
ai_type_application: Large language model-based chatbots for suicide-related query response and mental health support
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure to chatbot responses from Anthropic Claude 3.5 Sonnet, OpenAI GPT-4o mini, and Google Gemini 1.5 Pro for suicide-related prompts
comparator_control_group: Expert clinician-assigned suicide risk level for each query; comparisons across chatbot platforms
mental_health_outcome: Alignment of chatbot responses with clinician-rated suicide risk; direct versus indirect response to suicide-related questions; referral to professional help or hotline
outcome_measurement_tool: Clinician risk scoring scale from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high); manual coding of chatbot responses as direct versus indirect, plus coding of referral to friend/professional, hotline referral, and error message
positive_effects: All three chatbots avoided direct responses to very-high-risk suicide queries. ChatGPT and Claude provided direct responses to very-low-risk queries 100% of the time. When declining to answer, chatbots often referred users to mental health emergency hotlines or advised seeking help from a friend or professional.
negative_effects_harms: Chatbots were inconsistent for intermediate-risk questions. ChatGPT and Claude often directly answered some high-risk or lethality-related questions. Gemini often refused even very-low-risk epidemiological questions. ChatGPT often declined therapeutic questions and in some cases referred users to an outdated hotline predecessor rather than 988. The paper cites concerns and external reports of chatbots potentially motivating suicidal behavior, but this study did not measure actual patient harm.
evidence_type: Experimental simulation of chatbot outputs using hypothetical prompts with expert benchmark ratings; no human mental health outcome data
main_finding: LLM chatbots aligned with expert clinician judgments at the extremes of suicide risk, directly answering very-low-risk questions and avoiding direct answers to very-high-risk questions, but they did not meaningfully distinguish among low-, medium-, and high-risk intermediate queries and differed substantially across platforms.
effect_size_key_result: Compared with ChatGPT, Claude was more likely to provide a direct response (adjusted odds ratio 2.01, 95% CI 1.71-2.37, p<0.001), while Gemini was less likely (adjusted odds ratio 0.09, 95% CI 0.08-0.11, p<0.001). Relative to very-low-risk questions, odds of direct response were not significantly different for low-risk (AOR 1.03, 95% CI 0.07-15.17, p=0.99), medium-risk (AOR 0.11, 95% CI 0.01-1.15, p=0.07), or high-risk (AOR 0.12, 95% CI 0.01-1.76, p=0.12) questions. Very-high-risk queries received 0 direct responses across all models.

controlled_confounders.other_confounders: Mixed-effects logistic regression adjusted for chatbot platform as a fixed effect and modeled response iteration/question clustering as a random effect

limitations_bias: Limited to three commercial chatbots and late-2024 model versions; hypothetical prompts rather than real users; no measurement of actual suicide risk or mental health outcomes; no multiturn conversations; responses may differ with personal, informal, or vague language; mechanisms of refusals unknown and may be triggered by words like firearms or benzodiazepines rather than suicidality itself; expert benchmark based on a convenience sample of 13 clinicians; generalizability to other models and settings is uncertain.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as evidence on potential risks and safety characteristics of AI chatbots in mental health contexts, especially suicide-related support. However, it does not evaluate actual effects of AI on human mental health outcomes.
reason_for_decision: Useful for contextualizing AI safety and potential harms in mental health applications, but should likely be excluded from quantitative synthesis of AI effects on mental health because outcomes are chatbot behavior rather than human mental health.
notes_for_research_question: This study is about AI system behavior in suicide-related interactions, not clinical efficacy or psychological effects in users. It may fit a broader review of AI mental health harms, safety, or service quality rather than intervention effectiveness.

title: Problematic Social Media Use in Adolescents and Young Adults: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
study_design: Systematic review of cross-sectional studies with random-effects meta-analysis and metaregression
population: Adolescents and young adults aged 12 to 30 years
country_or_setting: Studies from United States, China, Spain, Turkey, India, Hong Kong, Lithuania, and Germany
comparator_control_group: No comparator intervention; associations between problematic social media use and mental health outcomes were examined
mental_health_outcome: Depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and stress
outcome_measurement_tool: Validated self-report instruments; Center of Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale was commonly used for depression, and Depression Anxiety Stress Scale was commonly used for anxiety. Stress also measured with validated questionnaires, specific instruments varied by study.
negative_effects_harms: Problematic social media use was associated with higher depressive symptoms, higher anxiety symptoms, and greater stress
evidence_type: Meta-analysis of observational cross-sectional studies
main_finding: Problematic social media use in adolescents and young adults was moderately and significantly associated with worse mental health outcomes, with correlations observed for depression, anxiety, and stress. Age, gender, and year of publication did not significantly moderate these associations.

controlled_confounders.addiction_problematic_use: Exposure specifically defined as problematic social media use measured with validated addiction-like/problematic use scales
controlled_confounders.demographics: Age, gender, and year of publication examined as metaregression covariates

limitations_bias: Only cross-sectional correlational studies were included, so causality cannot be inferred. High heterogeneity was present across studies. Number of studies per outcome was limited. Possible publication bias was suggested in some analyses though Egger tests were non-significant. Most measures were self-report. Clinical psychiatric diagnoses of participants were generally not reported. Study power was somewhat limited.
relevance_to_our_review: Low direct relevance for a review of AI effects on mental health because the exposure is problematic social media use, not an AI system or AI-based intervention. It may offer indirect background on digital technology and mental health risks.
reason_for_decision: This paper does not study AI exposure, AI tools, or AI interventions; it examines problematic social media use and mental health.
notes_for_research_question: Useful only as contextual background on non-AI digital technology effects on mental health among youth. Not appropriate as core evidence for AI effects on mental health.

title: Identifying and Categorizing Adverse Events in Trials of Digital Mental Health Interventions: Narrative Scoping Review of Trials in the International Standard Randomized Controlled Trial Number Registry
study_design: Scoping review of completed randomized controlled trials registered in the ISRCTN registry, comparing published protocols and primary results publications for adverse event reporting
population: Participants with diagnosed mental health disorders enrolled in randomized controlled trials of digital mental health interventions; included adults, young adults, children, and adolescents across multiple psychiatric conditions
sample_size: 23 trials
country_or_setting: International; trials identified from the ISRCTN registry across multiple countries and settings including health services, community, school, and forensic/prison settings
ai_exposure_intervention: Digital mental health interventions delivered via websites, apps, smartphones, computers, tablets, or virtual reality; interventions could be self-guided or supported by human contact
comparator_control_group: Varied across included randomized controlled trials; any control group was eligible
mental_health_outcome: Adverse events, serious adverse events, event seriousness, expectedness, relatedness, monitoring methods, and dropout reasons as potential indicators of harm
outcome_measurement_tool: No single standardized tool across studies; some trials used symptom checklists, Short Mood and Feelings Questionnaire, GAD-7, PHQ-9, modified symptom checklist, modified side-effects scale, self-report, therapist/assessor reports, session monitoring, and medical notes review
positive_effects: The review notes increasing recognition of adverse events in published protocols and suggests digital functionality could support standardized, automated harm monitoring and reporting
negative_effects_harms: Significant variation and likely underreporting of adverse events in digital mental health trials; only 6 of 23 trials reported adverse events in primary results publications. Potential harms included distress, deterioration, self-harm-related risks, app/device-related harms, cybersickness, exclusion or frustration due to digital eligibility or access issues, misunderstanding or misuse of intervention content, and dropout reasons suggestive of adverse events or serious adverse events
evidence_type: Review of registered randomized controlled trial protocols and primary results publications
main_finding: Adverse events are inconsistently defined, monitored, categorized, and reported in trials of digital mental health interventions. Although 16 of 23 trials mentioned adverse events somewhere in trial documents, only 6 of 23 reported adverse events in primary results publications, indicating substantial variation and probable underrecognition of harms
effect_size_key_result: Of 23 eligible trials, 16 (69%) included a statement on adverse events somewhere in trial documentation, but only 6 (26%) reported adverse events in the primary results publication; seriousness was referred to by 6 trials, relatedness by 4, and expectedness by 2
limitations_bias: Search restricted to ISRCTN-registered trials with both published protocol and primary results publication, excluding other registries such as ClinicalTrials.gov and likely higher-rigor or unpublished studies. The review did not assess risk of bias of included trials, did not explore trial standard operating procedures beyond reported documents, and did not deeply analyze specific adverse event types. Findings may overrepresent better reporting practices and do not directly compare online versus offline trials or digital versus nondigital interventions
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant for understanding harms and adverse mental health effects in digital interventions, but it does not specifically study artificial intelligence exposures or AI systems. It is mainly useful as contextual background on how harms are monitored and reported in digital mental health research
reason_for_decision: Exclude because the paper is not about AI effects on mental health; it is a methodological review of adverse event reporting in digital mental health intervention trials broadly
notes_for_research_question: Useful background source on harm reporting standards, adverse event definitions, and methodological gaps that may also apply to AI-enabled mental health tools, but not direct evidence on AI mental health effects

title: The Safety of Digital Mental Health Interventions: Systematic Review and Recommendations
study_design: Systematic review of published studies on safety of digital mental health interventions; included 17 randomized controlled trials and 6 pre-post studies, plus a secondary web-based postmarket safety search
population: Adults aged >16 years using clinical digital mental health interventions for conditions/symptom clusters including psychosis, depression, anxiety, body dysmorphic disorder, eating disorders, PTSD, suicidal ideation, insomnia, and loneliness
sample_size: 23 included studies; individual study sample sizes ranged from 7 to 3755
country_or_setting: 37 countries across included studies; most prevalent country United Kingdom; mainly high-income Western settings
ai_type_application: Digital mental health interventions broadly (mobile apps, websites/internet programs, virtual reality, social media-based interventions); no specific AI system evaluated
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure to digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) such as internet-based CBT programs, smartphone apps, virtual reality therapies, and related digital therapeutics
comparator_control_group: Varied across primary studies: treatment as usual, waitlist, supportive therapy, psychoeducation, healthy control, similar neutral intervention, similar active intervention; some studies were single-arm pre-post
mental_health_outcome: Primarily safety outcomes and harms of DMHIs, including adverse events, serious adverse events, symptom deterioration, increased anxiety/distress/depression, suicidal ideation-related harms, sleep disturbance, dependence, rumination, paranoia, traumatic memory triggering, and technical distress; efficacy outcomes varied across interventions
outcome_measurement_tool: No single tool; safety assessed via adverse event collection, serious adverse event reporting, self-report measures, standardized instruments such as Fear of Recurrence Scale, Symptom Checklist, PHQ-9, Inventory for the Assessment of Negative Effects of Psychotherapy, and bespoke questions
positive_effects: Review notes evidence that some DMHIs are effective and comparable to face-to-face therapies for common mental health conditions; some primary studies reported clinically significant improvement despite some negative effects
negative_effects_harms: Main reported treatment-related adverse event was symptom deterioration. Other harms included increased anxiety, distress or depression, increased sleep disturbances, triggering traumatic memory, unhelpful rumination from self-monitoring, increased paranoia, dependence on program content, feeling not taken seriously, technical difficulties, and one app-related serious adverse event involving hospitalization linked by participant to feeling overwhelmed by app installation.
evidence_type: Systematic review of primary intervention studies with qualitative synthesis and some secondary odds ratio calculations
main_finding: Safety assessment in digital mental health intervention studies is inconsistent and often inadequate. About one-third of included studies did not collect any safety data. Methods and frequency of adverse event assessment varied widely, formal statistical analyses were rare, symptom deterioration was the main reported adverse event, and risk mitigation mainly relied on excluding high-risk groups. The authors recommend standardized safety assessment, reporting, analysis, inclusion of high-risk groups with safeguards, and use of research safety data to inform postmarket mitigation.
effect_size_key_result: 23 studies included; 8/23 (35%) did not assess or collect safety data. 15/23 (65%) assessed risk. Only 6/17 RCTs reported sufficient data for odds ratio calculation. One reviewed study showed participants in intervention group were over 3 times more likely to experience an adverse event than controls (reported in review as OR 3.2, 95% CI 1.12-9.19).
limitations_bias: Most included RCTs had some concerns about risk of bias; more than one-quarter of included studies were non-randomized pre-post designs with confounding concerns. Safety outcomes were mostly qualitative, preventing meta-analysis. Only English-language studies and adult populations were included. Search terms focused on safety/risk language, which may have missed studies not explicitly labeling harms. Included studies were mostly from high-income Western countries, limiting generalizability.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as background evidence on harms and safety of digital mental health interventions, but not specifically about AI effects on mental health. Useful for contextualizing adverse effects reporting and safety monitoring in digital interventions more broadly.
reason_for_decision: Include only if the review accepts broader digital mental health interventions as adjacent evidence for AI-enabled tools; otherwise exclude because the paper is not specifically about AI applications.
notes_for_research_question: This is a review paper, not a primary AI study. It may help extract concepts on adverse events, causality, and safety monitoring relevant to AI mental health tools, but it does not isolate AI exposures. The paper emphasizes heterogeneity in adverse event definitions and recommends standardized safety assessment.
