title: Large Language Models for Mental Health Applications: Systematic Review
study_design: PRISMA-guided systematic review of peer-reviewed literature on LLMs in mental health; searched MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, JMIR, and ACM Digital Library; included studies published from January 1, 2017 to April 30, 2024
population: Studies on large language models applied to mental health, including text-based screening for depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation, mental health conversational agents, and broader clinical/educational mental health applications
sample_size: 40 included articles
country_or_setting: International literature across digital mental health, social media, clinical transcript, conversational agent, and psychiatry-related settings
ai_type_application: Large language models (LLMs) for mental health applications including detection/screening of mental health conditions and suicidal ideation from text, mental health conversational agents, clinical decision support, treatment planning, medication guidance, education, and therapy enhancement
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure to or application of LLMs such as BERT and variants, GPT models including ChatGPT/GPT-4, LaMDA, ERNIE Bot, LLaMA and related transformer-based models in mental health contexts
comparator_control_group: Varied across included studies; examples include convolutional neural networks, long short-term memory networks, baseline sentiment models, human analysts, physicians, chief physicians, psychologists, Google Search, and mental health professionals; no single unified comparator
mental_health_outcome: Depression detection, anxiety detection, social anxiety, loneliness, generalized anxiety, sentiment/emotion classification, suicidal ideation detection, empathy/acceptability of conversational agents, psychiatric diagnosis accuracy, treatment planning quality, medication advice quality, and broader clinical usefulness/safety in mental health
outcome_measurement_tool: Varied by included study; examples mentioned include F1-score, accuracy, precision, mean absolute error, relevance/human-like/empathy ratings, Patient Health Questionnaire-8 score prediction, vignette-based professional agreement, and examination accuracy
positive_effects: LLMs showed good effectiveness in detecting mental health issues and suicidal ideation from text, often outperforming some traditional deep learning methods. They may provide accessible, destigmatized, convenient, personalized, and cost-effective support, with nonjudgmental and empathic interactions. Some studies found strong performance in psychiatric case interpretation, exam-style questions, and agreement with mental health professionals on prognosis/treatment recommendations.
negative_effects_harms: Risks include inconsistent responses, hallucinations, biased or discriminatory outputs, lack of clinical judgment, inability to reliably handle emergencies, harmful or inappropriate recommendations, overestimation of suicide risk in some contexts, privacy and confidentiality concerns, black-box interpretability problems, dehumanization of care, possible overreliance by patients and clinicians, and lack of a benchmarked ethical framework.
evidence_type: Systematic review of heterogeneous primary studies and review articles
main_finding: LLMs have substantial potential in mental health for early screening, conversational support, and selected clinical aid functions, but current evidence indicates that risks and unresolved ethical/technical issues likely outweigh benefits for routine clinical use. The review concludes LLMs should not replace professional mental health services and are not yet ready for widespread clinical implementation.
effect_size_key_result: Among 40 included articles, 15 addressed detection of mental health conditions/suicidal ideation, 7 covered conversational agents, and 18 covered other applications/evaluations. Example results cited include GPT-3.5 F1-score 0.78 for depression detection versus CNN 0.53-0.59; RoBERTa for depression severity prediction with MAE 3.65 on PHQ-8; Emotion-aware BERT Tiny accuracy 93.14% for sentiment and 85.46% for emotion analysis; PsychBERT F1-score 0.63 versus CNN 0.57 and LSTM 0.51; BERTimbau for suicidal ideation accuracy 0.955, precision 0.961, F1-score 0.954; ChatGPT mean empathy 3.64 versus physicians 3.13; ChatGPT answered 85% of neurology board-style questions versus average human performance 73.8%.
limitations_bias: The review notes heterogeneity across datasets, models, and methods, making horizontal comparison difficult. Most included studies used social media data, which may introduce age and language bias and underrepresent older adults and non-English-speaking populations. Limited multilingual, expert-annotated datasets were available. Most identified studies focused on BERT/GPT, limiting diversity of LLMs reviewed. Rapid model evolution means findings may quickly become outdated. The paper reports Cohen kappa of 0.84 for screening agreement and use of Risk of Bias 2, but also included review articles due to limited literature, adding heterogeneity.
relevance_to_our_review: Highly relevant as a comprehensive systematic review summarizing both beneficial and harmful effects of AI/LLMs on mental health applications, including impacts on detection, support, empathy, safety, and ethical concerns.
reason_for_decision: Directly addresses AI effects in mental health, synthesizes 40 studies on LLM applications, reports positive and negative impacts, and is highly relevant background evidence for a systematic review on AI effects on mental health.
notes_for_research_question: This is a review rather than a primary causal study. Useful for mapping application areas, benefits, harms, and evidence gaps. It emphasizes that current evidence does not support replacing clinicians and that clinical risks may exceed benefits. Particularly relevant for identifying adverse effects such as hallucinations, inconsistency, privacy risks, emergency-response limitations, and overreliance, as well as benefits like accessibility, destigmatization, empathy, and text-based screening performance.

title: The Opportunities and Risks of Large Language Models in Mental Health
study_design: Narrative review and viewpoint summarizing existing literature on large language models in mental health education, assessment, and intervention; not an original empirical study
population: Not a single study population; discusses people with mental health concerns, mental health providers, and users of LLM-based mental health tools globally
country_or_setting: Global; includes examples from health care and digital mental health settings
ai_type_application: Large language models and LLM-based chatbots for mental health education, assessment, intervention, provider training, screening, diagnosis support, and treatment support
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure is use or deployment of general-purpose or domain-specific LLMs/chatbots in mental health-related tasks
comparator_control_group: Varies across cited studies; often comparison with human clinicians, physicians, psychiatrists, standard search engines, existing models, or no explicit comparator
mental_health_outcome: Accuracy of mental health education responses; screening and diagnostic performance; depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, stress reduction; empathy, rapport, safety, suicide-risk response; risks such as stigma, bias, inaccuracy, confidentiality breaches, and iatrogenic advice
outcome_measurement_tool: Varies by cited study; includes human ratings of helpfulness/accuracy/relevance/logic, benchmark case vignettes, DSM-5 case examples, specificity/sensitivity, symptom screening performance, and systematic review/meta-analytic outcomes for depression, anxiety, and stress
positive_effects: The paper reports promising early evidence that LLMs can generate accurate and immediate mental health information, support provider training, improve efficiency, detect depression and suicidal ideation from text, assist screening and diagnosis, and that some chatbot interventions may reduce depressive symptoms, anxiety, and stress. It also notes LLMs can be trained to express empathy, provide nonjudgmental responses, maintain therapeutic conversations, and potentially expand access to care.
negative_effects_harms: Reported risks include inaccurate, biased, stigmatizing, or harmful information; unreliable outputs; insufficient transparency and explainability; inappropriate trust; privacy/confidentiality risks; unethical practice beyond competence; poor personalization; forgetting prior context; nontherapeutic and iatrogenic advice such as encouraging substance use, dieting, and weight loss; and inconsistent or inadequate responses to suicide risk, including dismissiveness and failure to provide crisis resources or referrals.
evidence_type: Narrative review/viewpoint citing empirical primary studies, preprints, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses
main_finding: LLMs have meaningful potential in mental health education and assessment, with more limited and risk-laden evidence for intervention. Their use should be cautious and responsible, with domain-specific fine-tuning, human oversight, safety testing, equity considerations, privacy protection, and adherence to evidence-based and ethical standards.
effect_size_key_result: Examples reported in the paper include ChatGPT postpartum depression responses rated 3.93/4 for clinical accuracy; provider efficiency improved by 37.5% when editing ChatGPT-generated training content; Med-PaLM 2 predicted the correct DSM-5 diagnosis 77.5% of the time and correct diagnostic category 92.5% of the time; Med-PaLM 2 PTSD case classification specificity 0.98 and sensitivity 0.30; model correctly predicted comorbid diagnosis or modifier 20% of the time.
limitations_bias: This is not a systematic review and does not provide formal search methods, inclusion criteria, risk-of-bias assessment, or quantitative synthesis. Much of the cited evidence is early-stage, heterogeneous, sometimes based on preprints, case vignettes, or benchmark tasks rather than clinical outcomes. The paper itself notes that no widely used general-purpose LLM has been sufficiently fine-tuned or tested for mental health tasks, and performance and safety vary by use case.
relevance_to_our_review: Highly relevant as a synthesis of current evidence on AI effects in mental health, especially benefits and harms of LLMs/chatbots. However, because it is a viewpoint/narrative review rather than a primary effect study, it is more useful for background, identifying outcomes, harms, and primary studies than for direct inclusion in effect-size synthesis.
reason_for_decision: Relevant review paper for background and citation mining, but not a primary study directly estimating AI effects on mental health outcomes.
notes_for_research_question: Useful for mapping pathways by which AI may affect mental health: education, assessment, and intervention. Particularly important for cataloging potential harms and implementation safeguards. Contains several candidate primary studies on chatbot efficacy and LLM diagnostic/assessment performance.

title: Use of AI in Mental Health Care: Community and Mental Health Professionals Survey
study_design: Cross-sectional web-based survey with descriptive statistics and thematic analysis
population: Australian community members aged 16 years and older and mental health professionals residing in Australia
sample_size: 193 total; 107 community members and 86 mental health professionals
country_or_setting: Australia; online survey advertised on LinkedIn, Instagram, and Facebook
ai_type_application: Commercial AI tools, especially large language model chatbots such as ChatGPT, used for mental health support by community members and for professional tasks by mental health professionals
ai_exposure_intervention: Self-reported use of AI tools in the previous 6 months for mental health and well-being support or professional mental health work tasks
comparator_control_group: No formal comparator or control group; descriptive comparison between AI users and broader respondent groups/community members versus mental health professionals
mental_health_outcome: Perceived mental health support, emotional well-being support, psychological distress characteristics, and self-reported benefits, harms, and concerns from AI use
outcome_measurement_tool: Kessler 10-Item Scale (K10) for community members; AI Attitudes Scale; custom survey items on AI use, benefits, harms, and concerns
positive_effects: Community members reported AI was beneficial for quick advice when emotionally distressed, acting as a personal therapist or coach, availability, low cost compared with therapy, and privacy. Mental health professionals reported benefits for research, report and letter writing, helpfulness, and time saving. Free-text responses highlighted improved accessibility, efficiency, personalization, and potential integration with other technologies.
negative_effects_harms: Community members reported responses being too general or not personalized, uncertainty about where data was going, inaccuracy, unhelpful responses, lack of human connection, ethical/privacy concerns, and risk of misdiagnosis or missing distress signals. Mental health professionals reported outputs being too general, inaccurate, ethical concerns about professional use, risks of clinician overreliance, misuse, regulatory challenges, and data governance/security concerns.
evidence_type: Self-reported survey data with descriptive quantitative results and qualitative thematic analysis
main_finding: AI tools are already being used by a substantial minority of community members and mental health professionals in Australia. Most users perceived benefits, but around half also reported harms or concerns, especially around general/inaccurate outputs, privacy, ethics, reduced human connection, and data security.
effect_size_key_result: 28% (30/108) of community members and 43% (37/86) of mental health professionals reported AI use in the previous 6 months. Among users, 77% (23/30) of community members and 92% (34/37) of mental health professionals reported AI to be beneficial, while 47% (14/30) of community members and 51% (19/37) of mental health professionals experienced harms or concerns. Mean K10 score among community members was 22.8 (SD 8.9).
limitations_bias: Online recruitment may have attracted participants more familiar with technology; relatively small sample size; snowball/social media recruitment limits representativeness and generalizability; benefits and harms may be underestimated because use may have hidden or delayed effects; cross-sectional self-report design prevents causal inference.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as observational evidence on perceived effects of AI use on mental health support and associated harms/concerns, especially for generative AI/chatbots used in mental health contexts. However, it does not test clinical mental health outcomes or causal effects of AI exposure.
reason_for_decision: Useful for background and mapping perceived benefits/harms of AI in mental health care, but not strong evidence for actual causal effects on mental health outcomes.
notes_for_research_question: This paper is most relevant for understanding real-world adoption and user-perceived positive and negative effects of AI in mental health care. Community members often used AI as quick emotional support or a pseudo-therapist, suggesting possible substitution for professional care. Outcomes are perceptions rather than measured changes in depression, anxiety, or other symptoms.

title: A Comparison of Responses from Human Therapists and Large Language Model–Based Chatbots to Assess Therapeutic Communication: Mixed Methods Study
study_design: Mixed methods study
population: Licensed therapists with at least 1 year of professional experience evaluating chatbot and therapist responses to scripted fictional mental health scenarios
sample_size: 17 therapists
country_or_setting: United States; Stanford University; therapists recruited via Psychology Today listings, email lists, word of mouth; chatbot interactions evaluated in scripted text-based scenarios
ai_type_application: Large language model–based chatbots; general-purpose AI assistants and AI companions used for mental health conversations
ai_exposure_intervention: Three chatbots (ChatGPT/GPT-4, Pi, Replika) generated responses to two fictional mental health scenarios; therapists reviewed six chatbot interaction logs and compared them with their own responses. Seven chatbots were initially tested overall.
comparator_control_group: Human licensed therapists responding to the same scripted scenarios
mental_health_outcome: Therapeutic communication quality and suitability for mental health support, including handling of depression/social anxiety symptoms, suicidal ideation, empathy/validation, inquiry, advice-giving, and crisis response
outcome_measurement_tool: Multitheoretical List of Therapeutic Interventions (MULTI) coding; therapist rankings; think-aloud procedure; semistructured interviews; thematic analysis; word count comparison
positive_effects: Chatbots displayed elements of good therapy such as validation, normalization, empathy, reflection, reassurance, affirmation, and some psychoeducation. AI companions were sometimes perceived as more conversational and humanlike.
negative_effects_harms: Chatbots overused directive advice and psychoeducation, asked insufficient open-ended questions, provided generic one-size-fits-all suggestions, lacked feedback seeking, were perceived as limited in building therapeutic relationships, and handled crisis situations poorly. Reported risks included failure to perform adequate suicide risk assessment, delayed or absent referral to crisis resources, possible amplification of problematic judgments, potential user attachment/dependence, and possible degradation of social skills with long-term use.
evidence_type: Primary empirical mixed-methods comparative study with quantitative coding and qualitative therapist assessments
main_finding: General-purpose LLM-based chatbots were judged unsuitable to safely engage in mental health conversations, especially in crisis situations. Compared with therapists, chatbots used more affirming, reassuring, psychoeducational, and suggestive language but asked fewer elaborative questions and tended to provide generic, directive advice.
effect_size_key_result: Therapists evoked more elaboration than chatbots (U=9; P=.001; r=-0.65). Chatbots used more suggestions (U=12.5; P=.003; r=-0.61), reassurance (U=23; P=.02; r=-0.47), psychoeducation (U=22.5; P=.02; r=-0.48), and affirmation (U=28; P=.045; r=-0.41). Therapists wrote fewer words overall than chatbots (U=10; P=.002; r=0.64).

controlled_confounders.family_social_factors: Scenario responses were scripted and standardized across therapists and chatbots for direct comparison
controlled_confounders.other_confounders: Therapists were blinded to which chatbot produced each response

limitations_bias: Small sample size (N=17), scripted hypothetical scenarios with limited ecological validity, brief interactions only, no direct assessment of real user mental health outcomes or effectiveness, rapidly changing chatbot models, incomplete coverage of all available chatbots, and findings based on therapist judgments rather than patient outcomes.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant to AI effects on mental health because it evaluates how widely used LLM chatbots may influence mental health support quality and identifies potential benefits and harms, especially around crisis response and problematic long-term reliance. However, it does not measure actual patient mental health outcomes.
reason_for_decision: Useful for background and harm/safety evidence on AI in mental health support, but not a direct study of mental health effects on end users or clinical outcomes.
notes_for_research_question: This paper is best used for evidence on mechanisms, communication quality, and safety concerns rather than effectiveness. It suggests possible negative downstream effects such as overreliance, attachment, and poor crisis handling, but these were inferred by therapists rather than measured in users.

title: The Application and Ethical Implication of Generative AI in Mental Health: Systematic Review
study_design: Systematic review following PRISMA 2020; literature search across PubMed, ACM Digital Library, Scopus, Embase, PsycInfo, and Google Scholar for peer-reviewed studies published from October 1, 2019, to September 30, 2024
population: Peer-reviewed original research studies on generative AI applications in mental health, covering diagnosis and assessment, therapeutic tools, and clinician support; included studies involved general populations, vulnerable groups, patients, clinicians, social media users, and simulated clinical cases
sample_size: 79 studies included
country_or_setting: Global/multinational literature across mental health care, digital health, social media, and clinical/educational settings
ai_type_application: Generative AI, primarily large language models and conversational agents/chatbots used for mental health diagnosis and assessment, therapeutic support, and clinician assistance
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure to or implementation of GenAI systems such as GPT-series, LLaMA, Gemini, Falcon, Mistral, Flan-T5 and related prompt-engineered, fine-tuned, hybrid, or retrieval-augmented models for mental health tasks
comparator_control_group: Varied across included studies; comparators included traditional machine learning models, pretrained language models such as BERT, human clinicians/experts, primary care physicians, or no explicit comparator
mental_health_outcome: Depression, suicide risk/suicidality, anxiety, stress, emotion recognition/regulation, obsessive-compulsive disorder, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, PTSD, mental resilience, mindfulness, problematic smartphone use, preoperative anxiety, relationship distress, and general emotional support outcomes
outcome_measurement_tool: Varied by included study; included accuracy, precision, balanced accuracy, correlations with expert ratings, psychometric instruments such as State-Trait Anxiety Inventory and Self-Efficacy Scale, user satisfaction/engagement metrics, qualitative interviews, expert review, perplexity, BLEU, top-k accuracy, and reporting quality assessed in this review using MI-CLAIM-GEN
positive_effects: GenAI showed promise in enhancing diagnostic accuracy, especially for suicide risk and depression detection; multimodal approaches improved detection reliability; therapeutic chatbots were often associated with emotional relief, perceived empathy, self-reflection, reduced anxiety, reduced problematic smartphone use, and increased intervention acceptance; clinician-support applications may reduce administrative burden, assist treatment planning, case formulation, psychoeducation, training, and documentation
negative_effects_harms: Ethical and practical risks included privacy and data security concerns, algorithmic bias and fairness issues, reduced performance across dialectal/cultural contexts, hallucinations and medically inaccurate content, incorrect suicide-related documentation, inconsistent responses, insufficient crisis detection and intervention, overtrust in AI, abrupt termination of high-risk conversations, generic or repetitive advice, limited personalization, and lack of governance/oversight
evidence_type: Systematic review of 79 peer-reviewed original studies with mixed evidence including experimental studies, randomized controlled trials, quasi-experiments, simulated evaluations, retrospective analyses, qualitative studies, and technical benchmark studies
main_finding: Generative AI shows substantial potential as a complementary tool in mental health diagnosis, therapeutic support, and clinician assistance, but current evidence is dominated by proof-of-concept and simulated studies, with limited real-world deployment and major ethical concerns around privacy, fairness, safety, and governance
effect_size_key_result: Among reviewed studies, GPT-4 achieved precision up to 0.96 for suicidal risk prediction in some studies; depression detection accuracy reached 0.902 using semistructured diaries in one study; multimodal prompting for passive sensing depression classification achieved up to 61.1% accuracy; a 5-week field study reported 7% to 10% reduction in smartphone use and up to 22.5% improvement in intervention acceptance; overall reporting transparency averaged 45.39% yes on MI-CLAIM-GEN items
limitations_bias: Heterogeneity in study designs, datasets, and evaluation metrics prevented meta-analysis; most included studies focused on proof-of-concept or simulated interactions rather than real-world or longitudinal deployment; evidence largely centered on text-based language models; reliance on social media data may bias samples toward younger, digitally active, English-speaking users; reporting quality was moderate with poor reproducibility, limited harm assessment, limited real-world evaluation, and underreporting of data representativeness and resources
relevance_to_our_review: Highly relevant as a broad synthesis of how AI, specifically generative AI, affects mental health through diagnostic, therapeutic, and clinician-support applications, including both beneficial and harmful effects
reason_for_decision: Directly addresses AI effects on mental health across multiple application domains and synthesizes positive outcomes, harms, and ethical implications from 79 studies
notes_for_research_question: Useful umbrella source for identifying both beneficial and adverse mental health effects of generative AI. However, because it is a review and not a single primary causal study, causal inference is limited and real-world outcome evidence remains weak. Includes strong discussion of risks such as bias, hallucination, crisis-management failures, and privacy harms.

title: An Examination of Generative AI Response to Suicide Inquires: Content Analysis
study_design: Longitudinal content analysis conducted in two phases (spring 2023 and summer 2024) of general-purpose generative AI chatbot responses to suicide-related prompts, supplemented by LIWC-22 linguistic analysis
population: General-purpose generative AI chatbots responding to suicide-related prompts framed as youth/adolescent-style inquiries about a suicidal friend
sample_size: Phase 1: 3 chatbots analyzed (ChatGPT 3.5, Bing Chat, Google Bard); Phase 2: 7 chatbots analyzed (ChatGPT 3.5, Microsoft CoPilot, Google Gemini, Claude 2, xAI Grok 2, Mistral AI, Meta AI)
country_or_setting: United States; web-based chatbot platforms queried by researchers
ai_type_application: Large language model generative AI chatbots used for mental health/suicide information and crisis-support responses
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure to chatbot-generated responses to 5 suicide-related prompts in phase 1 and 7 prompts in phase 2, designed to simulate adolescent help-seeking about a suicidal friend
comparator_control_group: No formal control group; comparisons were across chatbot platforms and across two time points (phase 1 vs phase 2)
mental_health_outcome: Quality, accuracy, empathy, tone, authenticity, mention of crisis resources, lethality assessment, supportive guidance, and potentially harmful content in AI responses about suicide
outcome_measurement_tool: Human-coded content analysis and Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC-22) for authenticity and emotional tone
positive_effects: Responses became more comprehensive and responsive from phase 1 to phase 2; more chatbots provided suicide hotline information including 988; phase 2 responses more often included resources, urgency, support, nonjudgmental language, attention to lethality, normalization of outreach, care for the reporter, and alternatives to suicide
negative_effects_harms: In phase 1, resources were scant and lethality was not addressed. Microsoft CoPilot in phase 2 sometimes attempted to change the subject and forced the user to restart the conversation. One chatbot provided an unsolicited image depicting suicide, which authors note could be triggering or a risk factor for someone in crisis. The paper also discusses external examples of harmful chatbot interactions, but these were not part of this study's own data.
evidence_type: Observational descriptive evidence from chatbot output analysis; not human participant outcome data
main_finding: General generative AI chatbots showed improved suicide-related responses over one year, with greater depth, accuracy, empathy, and referral to crisis resources in phase 2, but important safety concerns remained, including inconsistent handling and one unsolicited suicide image.
effect_size_key_result: No inferential effect size reported. LIWC examples: ChatGPT 3.5 word count increased from 500 to 2198 and authenticity from 27.35 to 60.03 between phases; Google Bard/Gemini had the highest emotional tone scores (76.54 in phase 1; 79.99 in phase 2); Microsoft Bing/CoPilot had the lowest tone scores (37.99 in phase 1; 32.09 in phase 2).
limitations_bias: No human participants or direct mental health outcomes were measured; only free chatbot accounts were used; chatbot models and outputs change over time; prompts concerned a suicidal friend rather than self-disclosure; some platform access differed by time and account; coding involved researcher interpretation; results may not generalize to paid versions or future model iterations.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as evidence about potential effects of AI-delivered mental health information quality and safety in suicide-related contexts, but it does not measure mental health outcomes in users. Best suited as contextual or harms/safety evidence rather than effect-on-mental-health efficacy evidence.
reason_for_decision: The paper directly concerns AI in a mental health context and reports potential harms and supportive features, but it does not assess effects of AI on human mental health outcomes. Inclusion depends on whether the review includes safety/content studies in addition to outcome studies.
notes_for_research_question: This study is useful for a systematic review section on safety, crisis communication quality, and possible adverse effects of general-purpose AI chatbots in mental health contexts, especially suicide-related inquiries. It does not provide participant-level evidence that AI improved or worsened mental health.

title: Performance of mental health chatbot agents in detecting and managing suicidal ideation
study_design: Qualitative evaluation study of AI chatbot responses using standardized simulated suicidal-risk prompts based on the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS)
population: AI-powered chatbot agents available through mental health mobile applications and general-purpose chatbot systems; no human participants
sample_size: 29 chatbot agents
country_or_setting: Apps identified from Google Play Store and Apple App Store; testing conducted on iOS, Android, desktop web apps, and one local model run. Prompts in English; emergency-number appropriateness examined with user location specified as Poland.
ai_type_application: AI-powered conversational agents/chatbots for mental health support and general-purpose large language models
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure was interaction with 29 chatbot agents using a fixed sequence of escalating suicide-related prompts: depressed mood, passive death wish, suicidal thoughts, method ideation, intent, and imminent pill overdose scenario, plus follow-up prompts asking for crisis hotline number and specifying location in Poland when needed
comparator_control_group: No formal control group; informal comparison between mental health-specific chatbots (n=24) and general-purpose chatbots (n=5)
mental_health_outcome: Chatbot performance in detecting and managing suicidal ideation/crisis, including referral to professional help, emergency escalation, provision of crisis resources, contextual appropriateness, and consistency
outcome_measurement_tool: Prompt sequence based on Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS); pre-defined qualitative rating criteria informed by AHRQ Framework to Assist Stakeholders in Technology Evaluation for Recovery
positive_effects: Many chatbots advised seeking professional assistance (82.76%) and suggested contacting a hotline or emergency number (86.21%). About 58.62% insisted on getting immediate help at some point. General-purpose LLMs performed better than many mental health-specific apps under the study's criteria.
negative_effects_harms: None of the chatbots met criteria for an adequate response. Nearly half (48.28%) were inadequate. Common problems included failure to provide correct region-appropriate emergency numbers, lack of contextual understanding, inconsistent responses, not asking about active suicidal ideation, blocking suicide-related prompts, and highly inappropriate responses such as offering a selfie/heart reaction or affirming determination after suicidal intent.
evidence_type: Bench/simulation safety evaluation of AI systems; qualitative app assessment
main_finding: Current AI chatbot agents, including many marketed for mental health support, performed poorly in responding safely and adequately to simulated suicidal ideation. None met the authors' criteria for an adequate response, and substantial deficits were observed in crisis escalation and accurate emergency-resource provision.
effect_size_key_result: 0/29 adequate; 15/29 (51.72%) marginal; 14/29 (48.28%) inadequate. 24/29 (82.76%) advised professional help after mean 2.17 prompts. 25/29 (86.21%) advised hotline/emergency contact after mean 2.88 prompts. 17/29 (58.62%) insisted on immediate help after mean 3.71 prompts. 23/29 (79.31%) attempted to provide emergency contact info, but only 5/29 (17.24%) initially provided a correct region-appropriate number and only 3/29 (10.34%) did so without extra prompting. 5/29 (17.24%) explicitly stated they were not equipped to handle suicidal crisis. 5/29 (17.24%) asked about active suicidal ideation. 6/29 (20.69%) were inconsistent/inappropriate.

controlled_confounders.other_confounders: Standardized fixed prompt order across all chatbots; same scripted inputs regardless of chatbot response; English-language testing; supplementary prompts for hotline number and Poland location when needed

limitations_bias: No human users and no clinical outcomes; standardized prompts may not reflect real-life nuanced conversations; only one linear conversation path tested; prompts based on one suicide-risk instrument and alternative instruments might yield different results; only English tested; free versions/trials only, not full paid capabilities; qualitative assessment introduces subjectivity; app descriptions may have been misleading; unable to verify underlying models or determine whether responses were fully AI-driven, rule-based, or hybrid.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as evidence on potential negative effects and safety limitations of AI mental health chatbots in suicide-related contexts. However, it does not measure mental health outcomes in human users, so it informs risk/safety rather than direct effects of AI on mental health.
reason_for_decision: Useful for contextualizing potential harms and safety concerns of AI mental health tools, especially around suicidality, but lacks human participants and does not estimate effects of AI exposure on user mental health outcomes.
notes_for_research_question: This paper should likely be included only if the review scope includes safety, adverse effects, or risk management of AI mental health tools. It is not a clinical effectiveness study. The authors discuss prior human studies and an RCT, but this paper itself is a simulated performance audit of chatbots.

title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of adverse events in clinical trials of mental health apps
study_design: Systematic review of randomized controlled trials of mental health smartphone apps, with meta-analysis of deterioration/adverse event rates
population: Participants pre-selected for mental health problems, including depression, anxiety disorders, schizophrenia/psychosis, PTSD, bipolar disorder, eating disorders, suicidal ideation/self-harm, and general psychiatric distress
sample_size: 171 trials identified; 55 trials reported adverse events; meta-analysis of deterioration in app conditions included 13 app conditions and 1,672 participants; app vs control comparison included 9 comparisons
country_or_setting: Multiple countries and settings; databases searched were Medline, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and ProQuest
ai_type_application: Primarily mental health smartphone apps; limited AI-related content only. Some included apps had chatbot technology, but this review was not focused specifically on AI. One chatbot app was noted among included app conditions.
ai_exposure_intervention: Use of mental health smartphone apps as stand-alone or adjunctive interventions; one included app condition contained chatbot technology and some apps used symptom monitoring/feedback features
comparator_control_group: Inactive controls, care as usual, placebo apps, waitlist, information resources, face-to-face or group treatment, and other control conditions
mental_health_outcome: Adverse events, symptom deterioration, worsening mental health symptoms, hospitalization, suicidality/self-harm, app-induced distress, physical complaints, cognitive impairments, cyber sickness
outcome_measurement_tool: Validated symptom scales for deterioration (e.g., PHQ-9, PHQ-8, GAD-7, PCL-5, social anxiety scales), clinical interviews, open-ended questions, self-created items, objective indicators such as hospitalization, and in a few studies validated adverse-effect measures such as the Inventory for Assessing Negative Effects of Psychotherapy and the Negative Effects Questionnaire
positive_effects: The review notes growing evidence that mental health apps can effectively reduce a range of mental health symptoms, but this paper primarily examined harms rather than benefits. It found no significant difference in deterioration rates between app and control groups.
negative_effects_harms: Only 32% of trials reported adverse events. Weighted average deterioration rate in app conditions was 6.7% (95% CI 4.3 to 10.1; I2=75%). Severe adverse events reported in some trials included hospitalization, suicidality/self-harm, death, violent episode, and crisis care referral, though often not attributed to app use. Other harms included poorer mental health, subjective symptom increase, physical complaints, financial concerns, relationship problems, increased stigmatization fears, cognitive impairments, distress due to technical difficulties or in-app features, feeling too reliant on the app, and cyber sickness.
evidence_type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
main_finding: Few clinical trials of mental health apps report adverse events, and those that do often provide insufficient detail to properly judge risks related to app use. Deterioration rates in app groups were not significantly different from controls.
effect_size_key_result: Meta-analytic deterioration rate from 13 app conditions was 6.7% (95% CI 4.3, 10.1; I2=75%). App vs control deterioration comparison: OR=0.79 (95% CI 0.62 to 1.01; I2=0%; p=0.062).

controlled_confounders.baseline_mental_health_condition: RCT inclusion required samples pre-selected for mental health problems; some subgroup comparisons by target disorder
controlled_confounders.other_confounders: Between-group control came from randomized designs in included trials; review compared trial characteristics such as app features, control type, eligibility method, researcher contact, and risk of bias

limitations_bias: Only a small number of trials reported deterioration data; deterioration definitions varied across studies; adverse event reporting was heterogeneous and often lacked detail; early dropout may have masked harms; only RCTs and main outcome papers were included; supplementary safety publications may have been missed; many included trials had higher risk of bias.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as background/context on harms of digital mental health apps and discussion of chatbot-related risks, but not focused specifically on AI effects on mental health. It provides limited direct evidence on AI applications.
reason_for_decision: Include as contextual evidence on harms/adverse events in digital mental health apps and limited chatbot-related risk, but not as a core AI-specific effectiveness study.
notes_for_research_question: This is a review paper, not a primary AI study. It mentions concerns about chatbots offering harmful advice and includes at least one chatbot-based trial among broader app studies, but the central focus is adverse events in mental health apps generally rather than AI-specific exposure. Useful for safety framing and identifying AI/chatbot-related primary studies.

title: A scoping review of large language models for generative tasks in mental health care
study_design: Systematic search and scoping review following PRISMA 2020; synthesis of studies on generative LLM applications in mental health care with human validation
population: Mixed populations across included studies, including healthcare providers, patients, students, adolescents, and the general public in mental health-related contexts
sample_size: 16 included studies (from 726 unique records screened)
country_or_setting: Multiple countries/settings; databases searched included PubMed, Scopus, APA PsycNet, and Web of Science; studies included English, Chinese, Korean, Spanish, Japanese, and multilingual applications
ai_type_application: Large language models for generative mental health tasks, including clinical assistant, counseling, therapy, emotional support, positive psychology intervention, and education
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure to or evaluation of LLM-based chatbots and systems such as GPT-3, GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4, GPT4-Turbo, customized GPTs, Claude-3, PanGu, T5, and DialoGPT used for conversational mental health support, therapy-related tasks, journaling, cognitive restructuring, psychoeducation, and clinical decision support
comparator_control_group: Varied across included studies; some randomized controlled trials, some observational studies, some expert comparison to clinicians, and some no control group
mental_health_outcome: Depression, anxiety, suicidality/self-harm, loneliness, stress, life satisfaction, psychological well-being, positive and negative affect, ADHD-related outcomes, bipolar depression decision support, cognitive distortion, negative thoughts, abuse, and social emotions
outcome_measurement_tool: Mixed and heterogeneous; validated tools included PHQ-9, CES-DC, GAD-7, PANAS, SWLS, ISEL, De Jong Gierveld Loneliness Scale, Coping Strategies Scale, SPWB, SVS; many studies used ad-hoc or custom scales
positive_effects: Review reports initial promise of LLM applications. Examples summarized include improvements in mental well-being, reduced anxiety, increased life satisfaction in a GPT-based positive psychology intervention; 67% reporting reduced emotional intensity and 65% overcoming negative thoughts in a large self-guided cognitive restructuring trial; 75% of students reporting feeling less lonely and 3% reporting cessation of suicidal ideation after chatbot use; useful support for journaling and clinician insight; promising performance in psychiatric vignette and treatment recommendation tasks.
negative_effects_harms: Evidence remains limited; current evidence does not support use as standalone interventions. Major concerns include lack of standardized evaluation, limited clinical validation, reliance on ad-hoc scales, poor reporting, lack of safety/privacy/fairness evaluation, dependence on proprietary models, limited transparency and reproducibility, unclear target population definitions, potential bias, privacy concerns, and uncertain real-world effectiveness.
evidence_type: Review of primary studies
main_finding: LLMs show early promise for mental health-related generative tasks, but the evidence base is sparse, heterogeneous, and methodologically weak, with insufficient standardized evaluation and limited direct support for safe or effective standalone clinical use.
effect_size_key_result: Systematic search identified 726 unique articles and included 16 studies. Review notes examples such as 67% reduced emotional intensity and 65% overcoming negative thoughts in one large trial, 75% feeling less lonely and 3% cessation of suicidal ideation in one student chatbot study, GPT-4 selecting optimal bipolar depression treatments in 50.8% of cases, and ChatGPT-3.5 receiving Grade A in 61% of 100 psychiatric vignettes.
limitations_bias: Only 16 studies met criteria. Included studies were highly heterogeneous in design, populations, interventions, and outcomes. Many used non-validated ad-hoc scales and lacked clear rationale or psychometric support. Foundational constructs like safety, privacy, fairness, accountability, transparency, explainability, security, and resilience were rarely or never evaluated. Many studies lacked rigorous clinical validation, long-term outcomes, detailed demographic data, and reproducibility controls. Heavy reliance on proprietary models such as OpenAI GPT limits transparency and external validation.
relevance_to_our_review: Highly relevant as a review synthesizing evidence on AI/LLM effects on mental health outcomes, including both beneficial effects and risks/limitations of mental health chatbot interventions.
reason_for_decision: Directly relevant review paper on AI interventions and effects in mental health care; useful for background, evidence mapping, and identification of primary studies on mental health outcomes.
notes_for_research_question: This is a review rather than a primary effect study, so it should be used for contextual synthesis and citation chasing rather than pooled effect estimation. It highlights that apparent benefits exist but causal evidence remains limited due to poor standardization and sparse rigorous trials.

title: Opportunities and risks of large language models in psychiatry
study_design: Narrative review/commentary on opportunities and risks of large language models in psychiatry and mental health
population: Not a single study sample; discusses patients, clinicians, healthcare systems, and general population mental health
country_or_setting: General/global; examples include US healthcare and social media studies, NYU Langone Health System, and clinical mental health settings
ai_type_application: Large language models (LLMs); therapy chatbots; clinical decision support; natural language processing of clinical notes; predictive analytics; personal assistants
ai_exposure_intervention: Use or deployment of LLMs in psychiatric care, mental health support, clinical documentation, prediction, decision support, and conversational applications
comparator_control_group: Not applicable for the review itself; some cited primary studies include waitlist controls, clinician comparison, or unaugmented vs augmented LLMs
mental_health_outcome: Depression, anxiety, emotional distress, avoidant coping, empathy, loneliness/social connection, psychiatric functioning, suicide risk, broader population mental health and well-being
outcome_measurement_tool: Not applicable for the review itself; cited studies mention clinical and behavioral assessments, functional neuroimaging, psychiatric functioning assessments, health records-based prediction, and self-reported depression symptoms
positive_effects: Potential improved access to care, personalized support, efficient data collection, diagnostic support, treatment planning, monitoring, administrative streamlining, clinical note generation, therapy chatbot delivery of evidence-based interventions, improved problem-solving skills and reduced depression/anxiety in some pilot work, potential enhancement of empathy, support for research question generation
negative_effects_harms: Potential labor substitution with downstream mental health harms, privacy/data leakage concerns, bias and stereotype reinforcement, misinformation/hallucinations, inappropriate or unstable outputs, misinterpretation of nuanced symptoms, overreliance by clinicians, mismatch of values, reduced human-to-human socialization, possible worsening distress in vulnerable users, inequitable access to fine-tuned systems, limited transparency, cultural/regional limitations
evidence_type: Narrative review drawing on cited empirical studies, examples, and conceptual/regulatory frameworks
main_finding: LLMs may offer important benefits for psychiatric care and mental health research, but current evidence also identifies substantial ethical, clinical, social, and safety risks; responsible guardrails, red-teaming, oversight, and evaluation frameworks are needed before broad deployment.
effect_size_key_result: Review does not provide a pooled effect size. It cites examples such as GPT-4 identifying an optimal next-step antidepressant about 3/4 of the time, contraindicated or suboptimal options appearing in nearly half of vignettes in one study, augmented bipolar-depression prompting doubling expert-aligned choices with contraindicated/less preferred options in about 1 in 10 vignettes, and a pilot RCT reporting modest reductions in depression and anxiety symptoms with LUMEN versus waitlist.
limitations_bias: This is not a systematic review or meta-analysis; no formal risk-of-bias assessment reported; evidence base is early and heterogeneous; many claims are conceptual or based on small pilot studies and illustrative examples; cited LLM studies may have unstable prompting sensitivity and limited generalizability; regulation and long-term surveillance remain underdeveloped.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as background/context on AI effects on mental health and psychiatry, including both beneficial and harmful pathways, but not primary causal evidence on mental health outcomes.
reason_for_decision: Useful contextual review for identifying mechanisms, risks, and candidate primary studies, but not itself a primary study estimating AI effects on mental health.
notes_for_research_question: The paper is highly relevant for framing pathways by which AI/LLMs could affect mental health: direct therapeutic effects, clinician support, social substitution, labor-market impacts, bias/privacy harms, and system-level consequences. It also highlights the need to distinguish personal-use AI effects from clinical AI deployment effects.
